idiom_name: module-private sentinel object plus a runtime identity check (convention only)
implementation_notes: Python's tutorial is explicit that private instance variables do not exist and that name mangling is designed mostly to avoid name clashes - a mangled attribute is still reachable from outside. The closest structure is the module: keep the sentinel under a private name, do not re-export it, and let the restricted function compare identity and raise on a mismatch, accepting that this is a runtime check and that any caller can read the sentinel out of the module namespace. Real enforcement would have to be a real boundary, so use this as documentation plus a loud failure, never as access control.
pitfalls: Everything is public at run time: module._KEY can be imported and used to forge a key, and __all__ only controls 'from module import *'.
Identity checks fail confusingly after pickling, reloading or forking, because the sentinel is a new object per process.
Subclasses can override __init__ and skip the check, and object.__new__ bypasses initialisation entirely.
alternative: No enforced equivalent exists, so use the language's own convention as documentation: keep the operation module-private (leading underscore, __all__, a private submodule) and call it only from that module, or make the token a runtime-checked sentinel that fails loudly. If the boundary must actually hold, it has to be a real boundary - a separate process, a compiled extension, or a service that never hands out the implementation object. Python's underscore and __ conventions are not access control and must not be presented as one.
